From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

6. ## Executive view

The Seller’s package is materially buyer-unfriendly. Its combined effect is to:

1. disclose the entire data room and public record;
2. impute constructive knowledge to the Buyer and all advisers;
3. apply a **AUD 4.8 million cap and 18-month limit even to title, indemnity and other contractual claims**; and
4. leave several known liabilities or completion-critical matters unresolved until after Completion.

That combination could leave Wattlebridge owning the Company—and its problems—with little effective recourse. The Seller’s “standard market terms” characterisation should not be accepted without qualification.

Our review is necessarily based on the Seller’s summary and Disclosure Letter; the full SPA, schedules and DD-002–DD-012 should be checked against the points below.

## Material issues and proposed pushback

### 1. Limitations applying to “all Claims”

**Seller position:** Caps, thresholds, time limits, exclusive remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all claims of any nature.

**Concern:** This is substantially broader than a conventional warranty limitation regime. Depending on the definitions, it could cap or extinguish claims for:

- title and capacity;
- specific indemnities;
- tax liabilities;
- breach of pre-Completion covenants;
- failure to repay debt or release security;
- completion accounts or price adjustments;
- confidentiality and restrictive covenants;
- fraud, fraudulent concealment, wilful misconduct or deliberate breach;
- statutory misleading or deceptive conduct; and
- specific performance and other equitable relief.

It could even limit an obligation to return or adjust part of the purchase price.

**Pushback:** Limit clauses 12 and 13 to defined **general Warranty Claims** only. Expressly carve out:

- title and capacity warranties;
- Tax Claims and claims under the tax deed;
- specific indemnities, including Ironquay and the data incident;
- completion accounts, leakage and price-adjustment claims;
- debt repayment and security-release obligations;
- breaches of covenants and completion obligations;
- fraud, fraudulent concealment, wilful misconduct and deliberate breach;
- statutory claims that cannot lawfully be excluded; and
- specific performance, injunctions and other equitable relief.

Non-reliance and exclusive-remedy language must not operate as a disguised release of known misconduct or agreed risk-allocation provisions.

---

### 2. General warranty cap of 20%

**Seller position:** General warranty cap of 20% of price, or AUD 4.8 million.

**Concern:** Twenty per cent is at the Seller-friendly end, particularly when paired with broad disclosure, constructive knowledge and an 18-month survival period. Whether it is commercially acceptable depends on diligence coverage, the Company’s risk profile and any W&I insurance.

**Pushback:** Seek a general warranty cap of at least **30–50% of the purchase price**, or a separately negotiated W&I structure that does not leave material gaps. In all cases:

- title/capacity should be capped at no less than the purchase price;
- tax and identified indemnities need separate caps;
- fraud and deliberate concealment should not benefit from the cap; and
- Seller recovery obligations should not be confined to the general cap.

---

### 3. De minimis and deductible basket

**Seller position:** AUD 25,000 de minimis; AUD 250,000 deductible basket, with recovery only above the basket.

**Concern:** The thresholds are not necessarily unacceptable in isolation, but are adverse when combined with the low cap and short limitation period. A per-claim threshold could also prevent recovery for multiple related manifestations of the same underlying problem.

**Pushback:**

- Make the basket a **tipping basket**—once exceeded, all qualifying losses are recoverable.
- Aggregate claims arising from the same or related facts for the de minimis.
- Confirm the thresholds do not apply to title, tax, indemnities, covenants, leakage, completion adjustments or fraud.
- Ensure losses below the de minimis can count towards the basket if the Seller insists on a deductible structure.

---

### 4. Claim periods

**Seller position:** General Warranty Claims expire 18 months after Completion; limitations otherwise apply to all claims.

**Concern:** Eighteen months may not capture issues emerging through multiple audit, customer-renewal or regulatory cycles. It is clearly inadequate for title and tax.

**Pushback:**

- General warranties: **24–36 months**.
- Title and capacity: at least **six years**, preferably the applicable statutory period, with a purchase-price cap.
- Tax: the relevant statutory assessment/review period plus an appropriate buffer, commonly addressed in a separate tax deed.
- Specific indemnities: a period tailored to the relevant risk or until finally resolved.

A validly notified claim must survive expiry. Technical defects in a notice should not invalidate it unless the Seller suffers material prejudice, and contingent claims must be capable of notification.

---

### 5. Title and capacity

**Seller position:** Title/capacity subject to the same 20% cap and 18-month limit; reliance on the Company share register.

**Concern:** If the Seller does not own unencumbered title to all shares, the Buyer could lose substantially more than AUD 4.8 million. The share register is important evidence but does not replace contractual protection or verification of encumbrances and authority.

**Pushback:**

- Title/capacity warranties capped at **100% of the purchase price**, not 20%.
- Long-form survival as above.
- Confirm all shares are validly issued, fully paid, beneficially and legally owned by the Seller, and free of security interests, options, pre-emption rights and third-party interests.
- Require share certificates or satisfactory lost-certificate arrangements, executed transfers, corporate approvals and relevant PPSR/company searches.
- Require delivery of good title to be an absolute Completion obligation.

---

### 6. General disclosure of the whole data room and public registers

**Seller position:** Every fact “contained or referred to” in DD-002–DD-012, the Accounts, statutory registers and public records is generally disclosed.

**Concern:** This is not an acceptable substitute for fair disclosure. It shifts the burden to the Buyer to discover warranty exceptions, including matters only obliquely referred to. “Contained or referred to” could incorporate further documents not actually provided. Public-register disclosure is similarly open-ended.

The data-room cut-off is **5:00 pm on 22 September 2026**, which is now stale and may not capture subsequent developments.

**Pushback:**

- Disclosure should qualify a warranty only where made **fairly, specifically and with sufficient detail to identify the nature and reasonably foreseeable scope of the matter**.
- Require each specific disclosure to identify the warranty being qualified.
- Delete general disclosure of the entire data room and public records, or limit it to clearly identified documents that fairly disclose the relevant exception.
- Agree and attach a frozen data-room index and electronic archive.
- Require a refreshed disclosure letter and data-room update immediately before signing/Completion, without permitting late disclosure to cure breach or defeat termination rights without Buyer consent.
- Disclosure should not qualify indemnities, covenants, conditions precedent or completion obligations.

---

### 7. Buyer knowledge and “discoverability”

**Seller position:** No claim for anything known by the Buyer or advisers, including anything discoverable from the data room or public records.

**Concern:** This is a sweeping constructive-knowledge defence and, together with general disclosure, could make the warranties largely ineffective. It also imputes knowledge across an undefined group of advisers. Diligence should not displace the Seller’s contractual allocation of risk.

**Pushback:** Prefer deletion. If a knowledge limitation is accepted:

- restrict it to the **actual conscious knowledge** of a short list of named senior Buyer deal-team individuals;
- exclude constructive knowledge, matters that ought to have been known and adviser knowledge;
- place the burden of proving knowledge on the Seller;
- ensure mere access to documents is not knowledge;
- preserve claims under indemnities, tax provisions, title/capacity warranties and for fraud or concealment; and
- ideally provide that Buyer knowledge does not bar a warranty claim unless the relevant matter was fairly disclosed and expressly accepted in writing.

---

### 8. Bluefen consent—approximately 30% of FY26 revenue

**Seller position:** Reasonable endeavours; condition treated as satisfied upon delivery of written consent. No final consent or proof of satisfaction of its conditions is currently available.

**Concern:** This is a concentrated, completion-critical customer risk. A nominal consent may be conditional, revocable, accompanied by repricing or altered terms, or ineffective until clause 11.3 conditions are met.

**Pushback:** Make Completion conditional on:

- final, unconditional and effective written Bluefen consent;
- satisfaction or written waiver of all associated conditions;
- no termination, repricing, reduced commitment or other materially adverse amendment;
- consent being in a form reasonably satisfactory to the Buyer; and
- no material payment or concession by the Company without Buyer approval.

The condition should not be deemed satisfied merely by delivery of a document. The Buyer should have termination rights if it is not satisfied by the long-stop date. The Seller should bear the cost of obtaining it.

---

### 9. Riverlark debt and security

**Seller position:** Approximately AUD 3.2 million remains outstanding; release to follow Completion.

**Concern:** This conflicts with the agreed **debt-free/cash-free** acquisition. The Buyer should not fund Completion while the Company remains indebted or subject to bank security, nor rely on the Seller to procure a later release.

**Pushback:** Require at or before Completion:

- a binding payout letter;
- payment of principal, accrued interest, break costs and fees from Seller proceeds;
- irrevocable release of all Company and asset security, guarantees and related claims;
- PPSR discharge undertakings and subsequent evidence of registration; and
- bank confirmation that no further amounts are owing.

Use direct payment from Completion funds and, if any release mechanics necessarily follow, a sufficient escrow/retention. Completion should not occur without reliable simultaneous-release arrangements.

---

### 10. Completion bonuses—AUD 420,000 plus on-costs

**Seller position:** Bonuses are “a matter for the Seller” but are omitted from the funds flow.

**Concern:** If the bonuses are obligations of the Company triggered by the sale, the economic burden remains with the Buyer unless expressly dealt with. Payroll tax, superannuation and other on-costs could increase the exposure. This is a transaction expense, not ordinary post-Completion trading expenditure.

**Pushback:**

- quantify the full gross cost, including superannuation, payroll tax and other on-costs;
- deduct it from Seller proceeds or treat it as debt/transaction expense in the price mechanics;
- require the Seller to fund it at Completion; and
- obtain a specific indemnity for all bonus-related liabilities not reflected in the Completion statement.

Avoid double counting, but do not allow the liability to remain in the acquired Company without a dollar-for-dollar adjustment.

---

### 11. Ironquay IP—AUD 180,000 outstanding

**Seller position:** Existing indemnity is limited to the SOW3 payment.

**Concern:** The documents indicate transfer of SOW3 Project Materials is conditional on payment. This raises a chain-of-title issue over potentially business-critical IP. An indemnity limited to paying AUD 180,000 may not cover infringement claims, inability to use the materials, remediation, replacement costs, lost revenue or disputes about whether assignment occurred.

**Pushback:**

- Make cleared payment and delivery of an effective confirmatory assignment a condition to Completion.
- Require independent evidence of payment and Ironquay’s written confirmation that all relevant IP has transferred.
- Verify that the assignment covers all project materials, source code, documentation and improvements, and deal with moral rights, subcontractor rights and open-source components.
- Seller should fund the AUD 180,000 or it should be deducted from the price.
- Obtain a specific indemnity covering all losses arising from non-payment, defective chain of title, Ironquay claims and required remediation—not merely the invoice amount.

---

### 12. Data export/privacy incident

**Seller position:** Preliminary, not expected to be material; no confirmation of access, scope, notification obligation or loss.

**Concern:** The uncertainty is itself material. Approximately 1,240 records may be affected, and business contact information can still constitute personal information. There is not yet enough evidence to determine whether an eligible data breach, contractual breach, regulatory notification or customer-notification obligation exists.

**Pushback:**

- Require a privileged, independent forensic investigation covering access logs, download evidence, data scope, containment and recurrence risk.
- Require compliance analysis, including notification obligations, customer contracts and cyber-insurance requirements.
- Require prompt disclosure of all communications with the unintended recipient, regulators, customers and insurers.
- Seller to complete agreed containment/remediation before Completion where practicable.
- Obtain a specific indemnity for the incident and related investigation, notification, regulatory, third-party and remediation costs.
- Include a warranty bring-down and covenant that no further incident or material deterioration has occurred.

The Seller’s statement that it is “not expected to be material” should not qualify the warranties or replace evidence.

---

### 13. Supplier renewals—AUD 330,000

**Seller position:** Ordinary-course operating costs.

**Concern:** The Disclosure Letter itself does not establish whether the three related renewals are binding, unavoidable, accrued, terminable or attributable to pre-Completion periods. Their treatment depends on the actual terms and the agreed price mechanism.

**Pushback:**

- Review the three contracts and renewal notices together.
- Confirm service periods, termination rights, payment dates, prepayments and whether commitments were entered into consistently with past practice.
- Reflect accrued pre-Completion amounts in working capital or debt-like items as appropriate.
- Require Buyer consent to any renewal or variation outside the agreed interim operating covenant.
- Consider a price adjustment or indemnity if these are exceptional commitments made in anticipation of the sale.

---

### 14. Tax and IP under the general regime

**Seller position:** Both are subject to the general 20% cap and 18-month period.

**Concern:** That is inadequate for historic tax exposures and potentially fundamental IP ownership issues in an analytics business.

**Pushback:**

- Require a separate tax deed with appropriate conduct, payment and recovery mechanics, a substantially higher cap and survival through the applicable statutory review periods plus a buffer.
- Obtain specific IP ownership, valid assignment, non-infringement, open-source, employee/contractor creation and licence-compliance warranties.
- Give core IP ownership warranties a higher cap and longer period than ordinary business warranties.
- Preserve the Ironquay protection as a specific indemnity.

---

### 15. Office lease and Mossvale

The Disclosure Letter says the office lease involves notification only and Mossvale restricts assignment but does not expressly require consent to a share sale. Those legal conclusions should not be accepted without reviewing the full provisions.

**Pushback:**

- confirm there is no direct or indirect change-of-control trigger, default, termination right, repricing right or cross-default;
- ensure any required notice is given correctly and on time; and
- obtain a warranty that Completion does not breach either contract.

## Recommended negotiating priorities

### Must resolve before Completion

1. **Bluefen:** unconditional effective consent with all conditions satisfied.
2. **Riverlark:** simultaneous repayment and release of all security.
3. **Ironquay:** payment and effective IP assignment.
4. **Bonuses:** dollar-for-dollar Seller funding or price adjustment, including on-costs.
5. **Data incident:** completed investigation, remediation plan and specific indemnity.
6. **Title:** full title protection and delivery mechanics.

### Must change in the SPA

1. Limit the general cap, basket and time bar to general Warranty Claims only.
2. Remove constructive knowledge and adviser imputation.
3. Reject blanket data-room/public-record disclosure.
4. Preserve separate regimes for title, tax, specific indemnities, covenants, price adjustments and fraud.
5. Increase the general warranty cap and survival period.
6. Ensure notified and contingent claims survive the relevant expiry date.
7. Prevent non-reliance/exclusive-remedy language from defeating statutory rights or agreed indemnities.

## Bottom line

The Seller’s positions should not be accepted as a package. The most problematic feature is not any single number; it is the interaction of **blanket disclosure, constructive Buyer knowledge, a low cap, a short time bar and application of limitations to every type of claim**. Combined with unresolved Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, bonus and incident matters, this would transfer known and unknown downside to Wattlebridge without a corresponding price adjustment or effective remedy.

### 10. Completion bonuses—AUD 420,000 plus on-costs

**Seller position:** Bonuses are “a matter for the Seller” but are omitted from the funds flow.

**Concern:** If the bonuses are obligations of the Company triggered by the sale, the economic burden remains with the Buyer unless expressly dealt with. Payroll tax, superannuation and other on-costs could increase the exposure. This is a transaction expense, not ordinary post-Completion trading expenditure.

**Pushback:**

- quantify the full gross cost, including superannuation, payroll tax and other on-costs;
- deduct it from Seller proceeds or treat it as debt/transaction expense in the price mechanics;
- require the Seller to fund it at Completion; and
- obtain a specific indemnity for all bonus-related liabilities not reflected in the Completion statement.

Avoid double counting, but do not allow the liability to remain in the acquired Company without a dollar-for-dollar adjustment.

---

### 11. Ironquay IP—AUD 180,000 outstanding

**Seller position:** Existing indemnity is limited to the SOW3 payment.

**Concern:** The documents indicate transfer of SOW3 Project Materials is conditional on payment. This raises a chain-of-title issue over potentially business-critical IP. An indemnity limited to paying AUD 180,000 may not cover infringement claims, inability to use the materials, remediation, replacement costs, lost revenue or disputes about whether assignment occurred.

**Pushback:**

- Make cleared payment and delivery of an effective confirmatory assignment a condition to Completion.
- Require independent evidence of payment and Ironquay’s written confirmation that all relevant IP has transferred.
- Verify that the assignment covers all project materials, source code, documentation and improvements, and deal with moral rights, subcontractor rights and open-source components.
- Seller should fund the AUD 180,000 or it should be deducted from the price.
- Obtain a specific indemnity covering all losses arising from non-payment, defective chain of title, Ironquay claims and required remediation—not merely the invoice amount.

### 12. Data export/privacy incident

**Seller position:** Preliminary, not expected to be material; no confirmation of access, scope, notification obligation or loss.

**Concern:** The uncertainty is itself material. Approximately 1,240 records may be affected, and business contact information can still constitute personal information. There is not yet enough evidence to determine whether an eligible data breach, contractual breach, regulatory notification or customer-notification obligation exists.

**Pushback:**

- Require a privileged, independent forensic investigation covering access logs, download evidence, data scope, containment and recurrence risk.
- Require compliance analysis, including notification obligations, customer contracts and cyber-insurance requirements.
- Require prompt disclosure of all communications with the unintended recipient, regulators, customers and insurers.
- Seller to complete agreed containment/remediation before Completion where practicable.
- Obtain a specific indemnity for the incident and related investigation, notification, regulatory, third-party and remediation costs.
- Include a warranty bring-down and covenant that no further incident or material deterioration has occurred.

The Seller’s statement that it is “not expected to be material” should not qualify the warranties or replace evidence.

### 13. Supplier renewals—AUD 330,000

**Seller position:** Ordinary-course operating costs.

**Concern:** The Disclosure Letter itself does not establish whether the three related renewals are binding, unavoidable, accrued, terminable or attributable to pre-Completion periods. Their treatment depends on the actual terms and the agreed price mechanism.

**Pushback:**

- Review the three contracts and renewal notices together.
- Confirm service periods, termination rights, payment dates, prepayments and whether commitments were entered into consistently with past practice.
- Reflect accrued pre-Completion amounts in working capital or debt-like items as appropriate.
- Require Buyer consent to any renewal or variation outside the agreed interim operating covenant.
- Consider a price adjustment or indemnity if these are exceptional commitments made in anticipation of the sale.

### 14. Tax and IP under the general regime

**Seller position:** Both are subject to the general 20% cap and 18-month period.

**Concern:** That is inadequate for historic tax exposures and potentially fundamental IP ownership issues in an analytics business.

**Pushback:**

- Require a separate tax deed with appropriate conduct, payment and recovery mechanics, a substantially higher cap and survival through the applicable statutory review periods plus a buffer.
- Obtain specific IP ownership, valid assignment, non-infringement, open-source, employee/contractor creation and licence-compliance warranties.
- Give core IP ownership warranties a higher cap and longer period than ordinary business warranties.
- Preserve the Ironquay protection as a specific indemnity.

---

### 15. Office lease and Mossvale

The Disclosure Letter says the office lease involves notification only and Mossvale restricts assignment but does not expressly require consent to a share sale. Those legal conclusions should not be accepted without reviewing the full provisions.

**Pushback:**

- confirm there is no direct or indirect change-of-control trigger, default, termination right, repricing right or cross-default;
- ensure any required notice is given correctly and on time; and
- obtain a warranty that Completion does not breach either contract.

## Recommended negotiating priorities

### Must resolve before Completion

1. **Bluefen:** unconditional effective consent with all conditions satisfied.
2. **Riverlark:** simultaneous repayment and release of all security.
3. **Ironquay:** payment and effective IP assignment.
4. **Bonuses:** dollar-for-dollar Seller funding or price adjustment, including on-costs.
5. **Data incident:** completed investigation, remediation plan and specific indemnity.
6. **Title:** full title protection and delivery mechanics.

### Must change in the SPA

1. Limit the general cap, basket and time bar to general Warranty Claims only.
2. Remove constructive knowledge and adviser imputation.
3. Reject blanket data-room/public-record disclosure.
4. Preserve separate regimes for title, tax, specific indemnities, covenants, price adjustments and fraud.
5. Increase the general warranty cap and survival period.
6. Ensure notified and contingent claims survive the relevant expiry date.
7. Prevent non-reliance/exclusive-remedy language from defeating statutory rights or agreed indemnities.

## Bottom line

The Seller’s positions should not be accepted as a package. The most problematic feature is not any single number; it is the interaction of **blanket disclosure, constructive Buyer knowledge, a low cap, a short time bar and application of limitations to every type of claim**. Combined with unresolved Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, bonus and incident matters, this would transfer known and unknown downside to Wattlebridge without a corresponding price adjustment or effective remedy.
